source.title: Compositional Concept-Based Neuron-Level Interpretability for Deep Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Ze-Yu Jiang; Hai Huang; Xingquan Zuo

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses compositional neuron explanations to examine whether a neuron with multiple apparent activation conditions can be described by a coherent function, using a different method and in deep reinforcement learning.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure how common polysemantic neurons are, or test vision or language models, superposition, or initialization effects. Neuron 41 is explicitly described as multimodal and interpreted as monitoring a shared high-energy state. The architecture sweep measures neuron-concept alignment, not the share of polysemantic neurons; those results are recorded as findings that fit no version. The targeted perturbation experiments validate behavior effects, not polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: A DRL explanation-method paper that never addresses polysemanticity or superposition. Its only touchpoint is calling neuron 41 'multimodal' and glossing its disjunctive formula as a 'high-energy' state. That gloss is a post-hoc label on the method's own output, not a reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons with better tools. A J=0.999 disjunctive fit fits a single-function reading and a multi-feature reading equally well. So the results cannot bear on V6 or any other version. The width/depth sweep measures mean neuron-concept Jaccard alignment, not the share of polysemantic neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that their value-sensitive concept induction plus compositional matching yields interpretable neuron-level logical explanations in Blackjack-v1 and LunarLander-v3. They also conclude that targeted perturbations confirm these explanations are causal rather than correlational.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces value-sensitive concept induction and beam-search matching for DRL state features; it does not reproduce the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron-concept alignment varies with network width and depth; the paper reports monotonically lower alignment with greater width and optimal alignment at depth 3.

fits_no_version.finding: In LunarLander DQN agents, mean neuron-concept Jaccard similarity falls monotonically with width (64–512) and peaks at depth 3. All configurations solve the task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small DRL MLPs, wider networks show lower neuron-level alignment with compositional state concepts at similar reward.

record.code_released: The paper states that an implementation is publicly available on GitHub, but gives no URL in the provided text.
record.problems: The neuron interpretation evidence is based on a small set of highlighted neurons and two environments. The architecture plots provide no exact values in the text, and the study does not quantify the prevalence of unrelated feature mixtures.
record.rows_left_out: No results meeting the row criteria were left out.

rows.subject: DQN agent (LunarLander-v3), neuron 41
rows.size_stated: Three fully connected layers, 64 units each
rows.operation_detail: Matched a binarized neuron activation pattern to compositional concepts using Jaccard similarity.
rows.measure: Jaccard similarity between neuron activation and its best compositional concept
rows.note: The authors call the neuron multimodal because it activates for several conditions, including high altitude or high horizontal velocity, and interpret it as monitoring a shared “high-energy” state. They also describe rotational or moderate lateral movement while airborne as part of its formula.
rows.check: This is a method-output example, not a test of V6. The neuron is a DQN MLP unit, not a canonical vision neuron. The formula (ω1∨Vx3)∧¬RLeg∨Vx4∨Y4 lists several independent triggers. The 'high-energy' unification is the authors' verbal gloss, with no test separating one shared feature from unrelated features. Jaccard 0.999 measures formula fit, not monosemanticity.
